sections.title: The Opening Blessing and Living Hope (1:3-5)

blocks.text: The letter's opening blessing anchors the addressees' identity in Jesus Christ's resurrection. God's great mercy has caused them to be born again into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead. This new birth comes through imperishable seed—God's living and enduring word. The resurrection proclamation stands out as a startling theological claim in a world where death was typically final. In earliest Christian preaching, the resurrection vindicates Jesus and launches the hope of new creation. That living hope is bound to an inheritance reserved in heaven—incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading. The addressees are guarded by God's power through faith unto a salvation ready to be revealed at the last time.

sections.title: Trials and the Testing of Faith (1:6-9)

blocks.text: Though the addressees greatly rejoice in their inheritance, they presently endure manifold trials. This mingling of present suffering and future joy reflects the letter's genre: it serves as apocalyptic consolation. The testing of their faith, like gold proved by fire, is more precious than perishable gold itself. Their unseen but believed-upon Lord brings joy unspeakable and full of glory. The goal of their faith is the salvation of their souls, which they are receiving even now.

The addressees are exhorted to gird up the loins of their mind and set their hope perfectly on the grace to be revealed at Christ's coming. This exhortation rests on a command to be holy, invoking the scriptural language of holiness. The holiness theme runs deep in Scripture: it structures tabernacle and temple worship but also reaches into Israel's daily ethics and communal life. Holiness is not confined to ritual space but orders both worship and the conduct of daily life. The addressees, as God's elect scattered in diaspora, are called into this same holiness.
